before.attests_basis:
THIS IS NOT A MISSAL AND WITNESSES NO PRINTING OF ONE. It is a verse translation
of the hymns and sequences of the Roman Breviary and Missal, published at London
in 1849 with no imprimatur, no approbation and no decree in the front matter read
here. It names no Latin exemplar and it prints no Latin beside the English, so it
cannot say which book was on the translator's desk, and its English never had and
does not now have any liturgical standing.

The edge therefore rests on the date alone, which is the weakest kind and is
labelled as such, on the same footing as roman-missal-laity-1806, cummiskey-1843
and cummiskey-1861 in roman-holy-week-acts-v1.toml. 1849 falls after Urban VIII's
revision of 1634 and before Divino afflatu of 1911, so the state of the Roman
books it can be translating is the one si-quid-est-1634 left. It is drawn only
because a date bound is a real bound.

WHAT THE DATE BOUND IS WORTH FOR THESE FIVE TEXTS, and it is worth more here than
it would be for an oration: no act between 1634 and 1962 altered the words of
Victimae paschali laudes, Veni Sancte Spiritus, Lauda Sion Salvatorem or Dies
irae, and the Stabat Mater was appointed as a sequence in 1727, more than a
century before this book. The strophe-for-strophe correspondence against the
Latin this repository carries was counted for each of the five and is recorded in
the transcription artifact. So the recension question that governs the 1861
witness's Holy Week does not arise for this material -- which is a statement
about these five texts and must not be generalised to anything else in this book.
before.caution:
A LITERARY TRANSLATION, CHOSEN AS A VOICE. Caswall, Neale, Aylward and Bute
differ materially over these five texts. The active overlay records the
maintainer's choice of Caswall as the through-line across the relevant texts;
it does not argue that Caswall is right.

The English is metrical verse and is not a clause-for-clause rendering. Where the
Latin sets a short strophe Caswall may fold two into one six-line stanza, and the
stanza divisions in the text recorded here are his and not the Missal's. He
renders no Amen and no Alleluia anywhere: every one of these five propers ends in
the Latin with an acclamation that the English simply does not have.

Sing, my tongue, the Saviour's glory,
Of His flesh, the mystery sing;
Of His blood, all price exceeding,
Shed by our immortal king.
Destin'd for the world's redemption,
From a noble womb to spring.

Of a pure and spotless virgin
Born for us on earth below,
He, as man with man conversing,
Stay'd the seeds of truth to sow;
Then He closed in solemn order
Wondrously His life of woe.

Seated with His chosen band,
He the paschal victim eating,
First fulfills the Lord's command;
Then as food to all His brethren,
Gives Himself with His own hand.

Word made flesh, the bread of nature
By His word to flesh He turns;
Wine into His blood He changes;
What though sense no change discerns!
Only be the heart in earnest,
Faith her lessons quickly learns.

translations.text: Alleluia, alleluia. V. Hail, Queen of mercy; protect us from the enemy and receive us at the hour of death. Alleluia.

Let us all rejoice in the Lord, celebrating a feast in honor of the Blessed Virgin Mary, the Queen; at her feast the angels rejoice and together praise the Son of God. (In Paschal time, Alleluia, alleluia.) Ps. 44:2 My heart pours forth a good word; I address my song to the King. V. Glory to the Father.

translations.text: Eternal Shepherd, look favorably upon your flock and keep it under perpetual protection through blessed N. and N. (your Martyrs and) Supreme Pontiffs, whom you appointed as shepherds of the whole Church. Through the Lord.

May the abundant outpouring of your blessing come upon this lighted candle, we ask, almighty God; and, unseen giver of new birth, increase this nighttime radiance, so that not only may the sacrifice offered on this night shine with the hidden mingling of your light, but wherever anything from the mystery of this sanctification is carried, the wickedness of the devil's deceit may be driven out and the power of your majesty may be present. Through Christ our Lord.

We adore you, Christ, and we bless you, because by your Cross you redeemed the world.

By a tree we were made slaves, and by the holy Cross we were freed: the fruit of a tree led us astray, the Son of God redeemed us.

Savior of the world, save us: you who redeemed us by the Cross and your Blood, help us, we beg you, our God.

IV

1 and 2 Antiphon:

Faithful Cross, the one noble tree among them all; no forest brings forth its equal in leaf, flower, or fruit. Sweet the wood, sweet the nails; it bears a sweet weight.

1 Hymn:

Sing, tongue, the laurel of the glorious contest, and over the trophy of the Cross proclaim the noble triumph: how the Redeemer of the world conquered by being sacrificed.

2

Faithful Cross, the one noble tree among them all; no forest brings forth its equal in leaf, flower, or fruit.

1

The Maker, grieving at the deception of our first-formed father, when by biting the harmful fruit he fell into death, himself then marked out the wood to undo the harm of the wood.

2

2

Faithful Cross, the one noble tree among them all; no forest brings forth its equal in leaf, flower, or fruit.

1

2

Sweet the wood, sweet the nails; it bears a sweet weight.

1

The infant cries, laid within the narrow manger; the Virgin Mother binds his limbs wrapped in cloths, and a tight band encircles the hands and feet of God.

2

Faithful Cross, the one noble tree among them all; no forest brings forth its equal in leaf, flower, or fruit.

1

2

Sweet the wood, sweet the nails; it bears a sweet weight.

1

Behold, having drunk gall, he languishes; thorn, nails, and lance have pierced his gentle body; water and blood flow forth. In what a stream earth, sea, stars, and world are washed!

2

Faithful Cross, the one noble tree among them all; no forest brings forth its equal in leaf, flower, or fruit.

1

Bend your branches, tall tree; relax your taut fibers; let the stiffness given by your birth grow soft, and spread the limbs of the heavenly King upon a gentle trunk.

2

Sweet the wood, sweet the nails; it bears a sweet weight.

1

You alone were worthy to bear the world’s victim and, as an ark, prepare a harbor for the shipwrecked world—you whom the sacred blood, poured from the Lamb’s body, anointed.

2

Faithful Cross, the one noble tree among them all; no forest brings forth its equal in leaf, flower, or fruit.

1

May eternal glory be to the blessed Trinity: equal glory to the Father and the Son, the same honor to the Paraclete. Let all creation praise the name of the One and Three. Amen.

2

Sweet the wood, sweet the nails; it bears a sweet weight.
